title: Bone tissue, bone cells and growth
blurb: Label a long bone, tell compact from spongy bone, name the bone cells and explain how bone grows, remodels and heals.
question: After menopause, Rosa's bone density scan shows osteoporosis. Which bone cells are winning, which hormone change tipped the balance, and what kind of exercise helps?

teach.body: Formally, bone (osseous tissue) is a connective tissue whose matrix is about one-third organic collagen and two-thirds inorganic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite). In plain English: collagen makes bone slightly flexible and strong under tension; the mineral makes it hard. Bone has blood vessels, nerves and living cells, stores about 99% of the body's calcium, and houses red marrow, where blood cells form (hematopoiesis), and yellow marrow, which stores fat.

head: Part
What it is
rows: Shaft: compact bone around the medullary cavity
Ends: spongy bone with red marrow
Outer membrane: vessels, nerves, growth in width, repair
Thin membrane lining the medullary cavity
teach.caption: The metaphysis lies between diaphysis and epiphysis. When growth stops after puberty, the plate becomes the epiphyseal line.
Note compact bone forms the thick wall of the shaft while spongy bone fills the ends. The epiphyseal line marks where the growth plate was.
Osteon: central canal ringed by lamellae; osteocytes sit in lacunae linked by canaliculi; perforating canals join central canals.
Osteoclasts are large and multinucleated. Memory aid: blasts build, clasts carve.

head: Hormone
Effect on blood Ca²⁺
How
rows: More Ca²⁺ absorbed from the gut

teach.body: Bone is constantly remodeled as osteoclasts remove old bone and osteoblasts lay down new. Stress shapes it: weight-bearing exercise makes bone stronger (Wolff's law). Long bones grow in length at the epiphyseal plate and in width at the periosteum (appositional growth). When resorption outpaces formation, bone thins: osteoporosis, common after menopause as estrogen falls.

steps.label: Hematoma
steps.sub: Blood clot forms at the break

teach.body: Rosa, 64, learns she has osteoporosis. Since menopause her estrogen has fallen, so osteoclast resorption now outpaces osteoblast formation and her bones have thinned. Her nurse explains that bone responds to load: walking and light weight training stress the skeleton, and by Wolff's law bone strengthens where it is stressed. Adequate vitamin D helps her gut absorb the calcium her osteoblasts need.

teach.text: OsteoBLASTS build, osteoCLASTS break down. Adult red marrow is in spongy bone (flat bones, vertebrae, ends of femur and humerus), not in the diaphysis. Length grows at the epiphyseal plate, not the periosteum. Calcitonin LOWERS blood calcium.

items: Matrix: collagen for flexibility, hydroxyapatite for hardness.
Long bone: diaphysis with medullary cavity, epiphyses, epiphyseal plate, periosteum, endosteum.
Compact bone is built of osteons; spongy bone of trabeculae with red marrow.
Osteoblasts build, osteocytes maintain, osteoclasts resorb.
Flat skull bones and clavicles: intramembranous; most bones: endochondral.
PTH raises blood Ca²⁺, calcitonin lowers it; repair runs hematoma, soft callus, hard callus, remodeling.

summary: You can now label a long bone, contrast compact and spongy bone, and name the job of each bone cell. You can also explain growth in length and width, the two types of ossification, calcium hormones, remodeling and fracture repair.

A.q: Which bone cells break down bone matrix and release calcium into the blood?
A.why: Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells that resorb bone, releasing Ca²⁺ into the blood.

whyNot.0: Osteoblasts build bone by secreting osteoid; they are the opposite of osteoclasts.
whyNot.1: Osteocytes are mature bone cells in lacunae that maintain the matrix.
whyNot.3: Osteoprogenitor cells are stem cells that become osteoblasts.

A.q: Where does a long bone grow in length?
A.why: The epiphyseal (growth) plate of hyaline cartilage adds length until growth stops after puberty.

whyNot.0: The periosteum adds width (appositional growth), not length.
whyNot.2: The medullary cavity holds marrow; it is not a growth zone.
whyNot.3: Articular cartilage covers the joint surfaces and is not responsible for lengthening.

A.q: In an adult, the medullary cavity of a long bone's diaphysis mainly contains which tissue?
A.why: In adults the medullary cavity of the diaphysis holds yellow marrow, which stores fat.

whyNot.0: Adult red marrow is in spongy bone of flat bones, vertebrae and the epiphyses, not the diaphysis.
whyNot.1: Spongy bone fills the epiphyses; the diaphysis is compact bone around a hollow cavity.
whyNot.2: Hyaline cartilage is found at the epiphyseal plate and articular surfaces, not in the cavity.

B.q: Which structure is the basic structural unit of compact bone?
B.why: Compact bone is built of osteons (Haversian systems): a central canal ringed by concentric lamellae.

whyNot.1: Trabeculae form the lattice of spongy bone.
whyNot.2: A lacuna is the small space holding one osteocyte within an osteon.
whyNot.3: Canaliculi are tiny channels linking lacunae within an osteon.

B.q: Which hormone lowers the level of calcium in the blood?
B.why: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium, opposing parathyroid hormone.

whyNot.0: PTH raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts.
whyNot.1: Growth hormone promotes bone growth; it is not the calcium-lowering hormone.
whyNot.3: Calcitriol (active vitamin D) raises blood calcium by increasing gut absorption.

B.q: Which bones form by intramembranous ossification?
B.why: Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly in fibrous membrane: the flat bones of the skull, the clavicles and some facial bones.

whyNot.0: Long bones such as the femur, humerus and phalanges form by endochondral ossification.
whyNot.1: Vertebrae and ribs replace a hyaline cartilage model (endochondral), like most bones.
whyNot.2: The tibia, fibula and patella form by endochondral ossification.

C.q: Rosa, 64, has osteoporosis after menopause. Which statement best explains her condition?
options: Raised calcitonin has pulled calcium out of her bone
Her growth plates reopened and weakened the bone
C.why: Osteoporosis occurs when resorption exceeds formation; falling estrogen after menopause tips the balance toward osteoclasts.

whyNot.1: Osteoblasts winning would build bone and increase density, not cause osteoporosis.
whyNot.2: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium; it does not pull calcium out of bone.
whyNot.3: Growth plates become epiphyseal lines after puberty and do not reopen.

C.q: Which statement about the structure of a long bone is CORRECT?
options: The endosteum covers the outer surface of the diaphysis
Articular cartilage at the ends is made of fibrocartilage
The epiphyses are made mostly of compact bone and yellow marrow
The periosteum allows growth in width and fracture repair
C.why: The periosteum, the outer membrane with vessels and nerves, is responsible for growth in width (appositional growth) and repair, and anchors tendons.

whyNot.0: The endosteum lines the medullary cavity; the periosteum covers the outside.
whyNot.1: Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage, not fibrocartilage.
whyNot.2: Epiphyses are mostly spongy bone with red marrow.

C.q: Which sequence correctly describes the healing of a fracture?
options: Hematoma, hard callus, soft callus, remodeling
Soft callus, hematoma, hard callus, remodeling
Hematoma, soft callus, hard callus, remodeling
Hard callus, hematoma, soft callus, remodeling
C.why: A hematoma forms first, then a fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus, then a bony (hard) callus, and finally remodeling.

whyNot.0: The soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus forms before the hard (bony) callus.
whyNot.1: The hematoma is the first stage, before any callus forms.
whyNot.3: The hematoma forms first, and the hard callus comes after the soft callus.

reteach.title: Bone as a calcium bank
reteach.question: Think of your skeleton as a bank vault for calcium, with a demolition crew and a construction crew. Who makes withdrawals and who makes deposits?

blocks.body: Your bones hold about 99% of your body's calcium. When blood calcium falls, PTH sends in the demolition crew (osteoclasts) to break down bone and withdraw calcium into the blood. When blood calcium is high, calcitonin opposes that, and the construction crew (osteoblasts) keeps depositing new matrix. Osteocytes are retired builders living in the walls, maintaining them. If withdrawals outpace deposits for years, the vault thins: osteoporosis.

blocks.text: Crew names: clasts carve (withdraw), blasts build (deposit). Swapping them is the most common bone-cell error.

explain.body: The diaphysis (shaft) is compact bone around the medullary cavity, which is lined by endosteum. The epiphyses (ends) are spongy bone capped with articular cartilage. The periosteum wraps the outside, carrying vessels and nerves and anchoring tendons.

test.q: Which membrane lines the medullary cavity of a long bone?
test.why: The endosteum lines the medullary cavity; the periosteum covers the outer surface.

whyNot.0: The periosteum covers the outside of the bone, not the inside of the cavity.
whyNot.2: Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces at the ends of the bone.
whyNot.3: The epiphyseal line is the remnant of the growth plate, not a lining membrane.

explain.body: Compact bone is dense and built from osteons: a central canal with vessels and nerves, rings of lamellae, osteocytes in lacunae and canaliculi linking them. Spongy bone is a lighter lattice of trabeculae whose spaces hold red marrow.

test.q: In adults, red marrow is found mainly in which location?
test.why: Adult red marrow fills the spaces of spongy bone in flat bones, vertebrae and the epiphyses of the femur and humerus.

whyNot.0: Compact bone is dense; its canals carry vessels, not marrow.
whyNot.2: The adult medullary cavity holds yellow (fatty) marrow.
whyNot.3: The periosteum is a membrane on the bone surface and holds no marrow.

explain.body: Osteoprogenitor (stem) cells become osteoblasts, which secrete osteoid and build bone. Osteoblasts trapped in matrix become osteocytes, mature cells in lacunae that maintain it. Osteoclasts, large multinucleated cells from the monocyte lineage, resorb bone.

explain.caption: Osteoclasts come from a separate (monocyte) lineage.

test.q: Which mature bone cell sits in a lacuna and maintains the surrounding matrix?
test.why: Osteocytes are mature bone cells housed in lacunae; they maintain the matrix.

whyNot.0: Osteoblasts build new matrix on bone surfaces; once trapped in it they become osteocytes.
whyNot.1: Osteoclasts resorb bone on its surface.
whyNot.2: Osteoprogenitor cells are the stem cells that give rise to osteoblasts.

explain.body: Long bones lengthen at the epiphyseal plate and widen at the periosteum. Bone is remodeled throughout life, responding to stress (Wolff's law) and to hormones: PTH raises blood calcium, calcitonin lowers it, vitamin D increases gut absorption, and GH and sex hormones drive growth and plate closure.

test.q: A runner's leg bones become denser after months of training. Which principle does this illustrate?
test.why: Wolff's law: bone remodels and strengthens in response to the mechanical stress placed on it, such as weight-bearing exercise.

whyNot.1: Endochondral ossification is how bone first forms from a cartilage model.
whyNot.2: Appositional growth is widening at the periosteum, not a stress-driven increase in density.
whyNot.3: Intramembranous ossification forms flat skull bones and clavicles from membrane.
